data.title: Folliculitis — viva
data.summary: Bacterial infections · 15 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Folliculitis** (Bacterial infections)_

**Q1. Define folliculitis and classify it.**
- Inflammation of the hair follicle (infective or non-infective)
- By depth: superficial (ostial — Bockhart's) vs deep (sycosis, furuncle, carbuncle)
- By cause: bacterial (S. aureus, Pseudomonas 'hot-tub', Gram-negative in acne on long antibiotics), fungal (Pityrosporum/Malassezia, dermatophytic Majocchi's granuloma, Candida), viral (herpetic, molluscum), parasitic (Demodex), non-infective (eosinophilic, pseudofolliculitis barbae, perforating, actinic, drug-induced — EGFR inhibitors, steroids)

**Q2. Describe Bockhart's (superficial) folliculitis.**
- Small dome-shaped pustules pierced by a hair, on scalp, beard, limbs, buttocks; heal without scars
- Predisposed by shaving, occlusion, sweating, oils, topical steroids

**Q3. What is sycosis barbae? How does it differ from tinea barbae?**
- Chronic deep follicular staphylococcal infection of the beard area in men; perifollicular papules/pustules that recur, with crusting; hair pulls out with difficulty
- Tinea barbae: zoophilic dermatophyte, usually unilateral, kerion-like boggy plaques, hairs loose and easily pulled out, KOH positive; upper lip usually spared in tinea and involved in sycosis

**Q4. What is lupoid sycosis?**
- Chronic scarring form of sycosis with central atrophic scar and peripheral pustules — resembles lupus vulgaris

**Q5. Differentiate pseudofolliculitis barbae from sycosis.**
- Pseudofolliculitis is a foreign-body reaction to curved hairs re-entering skin after close shaving — common in tightly curled hair; papules with embedded hair, sterile
- Treatment: stop close shaving, laser hair removal, topical retinoid, mild steroid

**Q6. What is hot-tub folliculitis?**
- Pseudomonas aeruginosa from poorly chlorinated pools/tubs; itchy follicular papulopustules on areas covered by swimwear, 1–2 days after exposure
- Self-limiting in 7–10 days; ciprofloxacin if severe

**Q7. Describe Pityrosporum (Malassezia) folliculitis.**
- Itchy monomorphic follicular papules and pustules on upper back, chest, shoulders in young adults; after antibiotics, steroids, humidity, diabetes
- KOH: round budding yeasts in follicles (no hyphae); responds to azoles (topical ketoconazole, oral itraconazole/fluconazole), not to antibiotics
- Differential: acne vulgaris (comedones, polymorphous)

**Q8. What is Gram-negative folliculitis?**
- Complication of long-term tetracycline in acne: Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Proteus — pustules around nose and chin, or deep nodules
- Treat with isotretinoin (best) or culture-directed antibiotic

**Q9. What is eosinophilic pustular folliculitis? Name its types.**
- Ofuji type (classic, Japanese adults; annular plaques of sterile follicular pustules on face/trunk)
- HIV-associated (very itchy; CD4 <250; improves with ART)
- Infantile (scalp)
- Treatment: indomethacin (Ofuji responds dramatically), phototherapy, antihistamines, topical steroids

**Q10. What is folliculitis decalvans?**
- Chronic neutrophilic scarring alopecia of vertex/occiput with tufted hairs (polytrichia), pustules and crusts; S. aureus has a role
- Treatment: rifampicin + clindamycin (10 weeks), doxycycline, dapsone, isotretinoin, intralesional steroid

**Q11. What is Majocchi's granuloma?**
- Dermatophyte invading follicles and the dermis — often after topical steroid on tinea; legs of women who shave
- Needs oral antifungal

**Q12. Name the drugs that cause acneiform or folliculitis-like eruptions.**
- Corticosteroids, androgens, lithium, isoniazid, phenytoin, halogens (iodides, bromides), EGFR inhibitors (cetuximab, erlotinib, gefitinib), MEK inhibitors, vitamin B12, cyclosporine
- Monomorphic; usually no comedones

**Q13. How do you manage recurrent staphylococcal folliculitis?**
- Swab nares, axillae, perineum for carriage; treat diabetes, obesity, iron deficiency, immunodeficiency
- Decolonisation: nasal mupirocin twice daily 5 days monthly, chlorhexidine or dilute bleach baths, wash linen in hot water
- Topical clindamycin/benzoyl peroxide; oral cloxacillin/cephalexin; for recurrent: clindamycin, or rifampicin combined with another drug (never alone)
- Avoid shaving against grain, occlusive clothing

**Q14. How do you investigate folliculitis?**
- Gram stain and culture of pus; KOH for fungi; Demodex mount (standardised skin surface biopsy)
- Biopsy in non-responders (eosinophilic, perforating)
- Blood sugar, HIV if indicated

**Q15. What is Demodex folliculitis?**
- Rosacea-like facial papulopustules with heavy Demodex load (>5 mites/cm²); immunosuppressed and topical steroid users
- Treatment: ivermectin 1% cream, permethrin, metronidazole, oral ivermectin

## Quick spotter facts
- Upper lip involved — sycosis; spared — tinea barbae
- Monomorphic itchy back pustules, no comedones — think Pityrosporum folliculitis

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (ch. Pyodermas); Rook's Textbook of Dermatology for cross-check. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
